topic: Google Cloud Generative AI Leader certification exam preparation - Google Cloud's foundational credential for leaders and professionals who shape, guide, and evangelize generative AI strategy and adoption using the Google Cloud and Gemini ecosystem
cert_name: Google Cloud Certified - Generative AI Leader
exam_format: 50-60 multiple-choice and multiple-select questions, 90 minutes, taken via online-proctored or onsite test center. No prerequisites and no hands-on coding required - this is a foundational, strategy-and-concepts exam. Google does not publish an official numeric pass score (scaled pass/fail). The credential is valid for 3 years. Aimed at business and technical leaders rather than builders.
question_types: multiple choice (single answer, exactly 4 options) and multiple select clearly marked as 'Select TWO/THREE'
audience: Business leaders, product managers, cloud strategists, enterprise architects, consultants, and technical professionals who need to identify gen AI use cases, shape AI strategy, and lead responsible adoption - regardless of hands-on coding experience. A strong first Google Cloud credential and a natural companion to vendor-neutral governance courses like AIGP. No coding background required.
author: Aseem Mankotia

domains.name: Fundamentals of generative AI
domains.notes: Core concepts and vocabulary a leader must speak fluently: what generative AI is and how it differs from traditional/predictive ML; foundation models and large language models; how models are trained (pre-training, training data, parameters) and how inference works; tokens, embeddings, and context windows; multimodal models (text, image, audio, video, code); the transformer idea at a conceptual (non-math) level; common failure modes such as hallucination, bias, and knowledge cutoffs; prompt engineering as a first lever; Google's Responsible AI principles and the concepts of fairness, safety, privacy, transparency, and human oversight. Framing: what gen AI is good and bad at, and how to set realistic expectations with stakeholders.

domains.name: Google Cloud's generative AI offerings
domains.notes: The largest domain - the Google gen AI product map. Gemini models and the Gemini app; Gemini for Google Workspace (Docs, Sheets, Gmail, Meet); Vertex AI as the enterprise platform, including Vertex AI Studio and Model Garden (access to Gemini plus third-party and open models); Vertex AI Agent Builder and Agentspace for building and deploying agents; NotebookLM / NotebookLM Enterprise; Gemini Code Assist for developers; grounding with Google Search and with enterprise data; Google Cloud's AI-optimized infrastructure (TPUs and GPUs) and why it matters for scale and cost; how the pieces fit into a solution and when a leader would choose the managed app experience versus the Vertex AI platform versus custom development. Emphasize choosing the RIGHT Google tool for a described business scenario.

domains.name: Techniques to improve gen AI model output
domains.notes: The levers that turn a generic model into a reliable business solution, at a conceptual level: prompt engineering (zero-shot, few-shot, role and system prompts, chain-of-thought); grounding and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to reduce hallucination and connect models to current or proprietary data; embeddings and vector search; fine-tuning and when it is (and is not) worth it versus prompting or RAG; sampling controls such as temperature and top-k/top-p in plain language; context and context windows; and how to evaluate output quality, groundedness, and safety. A leader should be able to recommend grounding vs fine-tuning vs prompt changes for a given accuracy or freshness problem.

domains.name: Business strategies for a successful gen AI solution
domains.notes: Turning capability into value: identifying and prioritizing high-value gen AI use cases; building a gen AI strategy aligned to business goals; measuring ROI and business impact; managing organizational change, adoption, and workforce upskilling; responsible AI governance, risk management, security, data privacy, and compliance as leadership responsibilities; cost awareness and scaling considerations; the role of human-in-the-loop and accountability. Scenario framing: defending an AI investment, choosing a first use case, and reducing operational and reputational risk.

extra_guidance: This is a FOUNDATIONAL, leader-oriented exam - the course must stay strategic and conceptual, never turning into a coding tutorial. Marketing angle: 'the AI certification for people who lead AI, not just build it' and 'your first Google Cloud credential.' This is the portfolio's first Google Cloud course, so lean into the Google/Gemini/Vertex AI keyword cluster for SEO. The four domain names and weights above are Google's official exam-guide domains - use them verbatim. Because the audience is non-technical leaders, every technical concept must be explained with a business analogy and a 'why this matters to you' framing; avoid Python and avoid API syntax entirely. Keep Google product naming current (Gemini app, Gemini for Google Workspace, Vertex AI, Vertex AI Studio, Model Garden, Vertex AI Agent Builder, Agentspace, NotebookLM Enterprise, Gemini Code Assist) and note that Google renames offerings frequently, so teach the CATEGORY (managed app vs platform vs agent builder vs grounding) alongside the current brand name. 'Labs' should be light, no-code walkthroughs: exploring Vertex AI Studio in the console, trying a prompt in the Gemini app, sketching a RAG grounding flow, and mapping a business use case to the right Google tool. Practice tests must be scenario-heavy: 'a company wants X, which Google offering fits?', 'output is outdated/hallucinating - grounding, RAG, or fine-tuning?', 'which Responsible AI principle applies?', and ROI/strategy judgment calls. Cover classic distinctions leaders confuse: Gemini app vs Vertex AI, grounding vs fine-tuning vs prompt engineering, RAG vs fine-tuning, foundation model vs fine-tuned model, and predictive ML vs generative AI. Since there is no published numeric pass score, do NOT promise a specific score; use exam-focused, readiness framing only. Final chapter must be a full exam simulation walkthrough with a 90-minute time-management strategy for 50-60 questions.
